utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to the rest of you. General Miletic is back. Hope he is feeling well. You are all right now? Yeah, okay. Thank you. But we have accused Popovic absent. He had given prior notice of that, and we are in possession, also, of the waiver. Prosecution, same situation as yesterday: Mr. McCloskey Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Elderkin. And Defence teams, also same as yesterday: Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Haynes absent, and Mr. Lazarevic. Good morning to you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I'm confident we will finish with your testimony today, and in any case I will need about ten minutes towards the end to, again, deal with some housekeeping matters in case we -- so we have to accelerate, then, your cross-examination, okay? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning again, Professor.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'm going to do now is just ask you a couple questions about how the report was actually created and drafted and the summaries and then try to go right into the guts of the report. Could we have 3696 up, please, on e-court. Those are the summaries, but the first page should not be broadcast. If we go right to page 7, that should be Major Boering, then there should be no problem. The first page has the names of protected witnesses. Thank you. Now, very simply and briefly, Professor, these are the summaries that we were talking about that were created in preparation for the report, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And these were written, you said, with a colleague from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Philip De Man --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Philip De Man. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who was the case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just very briefly help me understand how these were created, sitting down talking, who typed them up, that kind of thing. Just give us an idea.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained, the first step was that I asked for parts of the case file that were relevant to a number of topics, like familiarity, meeting people, possible recognition and identification tests. We went together through those sheets and marked the passages that I thought were relevant, and these passages were summarized in these summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These summaries were then collected. I made already made my own notes that you also have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- received, which are, again, abstract from these summaries, and then in the report you find a table, which is, again, an abstract from these notes. The business of scientific analysis is to a large extent data reduction and further data reduction, so usually there are a number of steps where you make the things smaller and smaller, and this is one of the intermediate products that you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that, and if we could have your report up, which is 2D574, page 9. We don't necessarily need to bring it up, but I'm discussing now the table which you just talked about, and I think you said, I don't have the cite here, that you also created this -- that's not the correct page. It's page 9 in my copy. That's right. Sorry, at 25182 in the transcript you said that this table was made with a colleague. Could you just tell me how that was done, who entered the data into this table, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table was made by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just by you?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you typed --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the notes that I transferred yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, so all these the typing we see here, you physically put that in yourself?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comes from my machine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm done with that. I'm now going to ask you about part 2 of your report, which is the part where after giving us the rules you then begin to analyse the specifics of this case. And you analyse the situation for 12 witnesses. You went through this yesterday, but I'll just quickly summarize it so we can see where I'm going. 3 of the 12 witnesses were classified as familiar with Mr. Beara, therefore should not have been given lineup tests, and those are Milorad Bircakovic, Mr. Celanovic, and PW 161, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's -- they are classified by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. By no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. I'm not suggesting otherwise. Two witnesses you explained very well yesterday according to the material provided to you may have seen Mr. Beara after the encounter in question, therefore, should not have been tested, PW 162 and Mr. Peric, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So we are left with seven witnesses, which as you state in your report you did not find in the materials made available to you "any indication why it was impossible, undesirable, or unnecessary to test the claims of the witnesses that they saw Mr. Beara in the various situations described by them." That's from Section 2(C) of your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 2(2), excuse me. And just so we're clear, I'm going to go through those seven now. Those are Mr. Babic, Mr. Erdemovic, PW 165, Major Boering, Mr. Egbers, Milosevic, and PW 104, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to now start talking about those witnesses in the order they appear in your table, meaning that the first one is PW 165. He is the first one on your table.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He testified on the 3rd and 4th of April, 2007, and as you will know from the materials provided to you by the Defence, you had his interview - coincidentally done by me - and he was interviewed on the 26th of November, 2005. You've got in your table -- or sorry, not in your table, but beside saying he's one of the ones who could or should have been tested, you say in the last paragraph of your report that "because he did not describe Beara as wearing glasses, there was all the more reason to do a lineup."

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at what PW 165 said in this trial about his encounter with Mr. Beara. Says 4th of April, 2007, at page 9962. "Question: Did you see any security officer standard at the Zvornik brigade headquarters that evening? "Answer: Well, that evening when I arrived, when I arrived to the premises of our company, up the stairs there were a few people walking around, and they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and I saw their backs, and I asked who that was, and one of them said, well, the commander has a meeting with Popovic and Beara." And you've put that in your Column 3 that PW 165 saw him maybe once. This is what else it says in the transcripts provided to you by the Defence, page 9965: "Question: Okay, and you said he was with somebody named Beara. Did you know this person Beara in that time in July 1995? "Answer: No, never, nor did I ever see him. Never." Again, 9979, cross-examination. You state that you never saw him before, and the person you were referencing there is Mr. Beara, correct? You never saw him before during that purported visit or after that visit; is that correct? "Answer: Yes, that's correct. I never saw him. "Neither before or afterwards nor during the purported meeting at the Zvornik brigade headquarters, correct? "I've already said that. Yes, that is correct."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down a little bit for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm going to -- I'm not just reading this. I'm going to ask you a question in a minute. This is what the witness says about his exposure to the media regarding ICTY Srebrenica defendants after the 15 July 1995 encounter at the Zvornik brigade headquarters. At 9967, do you remember that saying that he saw Vujadin Popovic on TV in a television programme? He said he heard about the warrant for Vujadin Popovic who shares this indictment with Mr. Beara. And you were given, it's in your materials, a copy of PW 165's second statement. That's dated 22nd of March, 2007. That's 65 ter number 3662. If we could bring that up, please, on page 2. Now, here, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Here -- I am sorry that shouldn't be broadcast. I'll read it to you, Professor, paragraph 4, and here Mr. PW 165 is correcting or commenting on his first statement, and he says regarding paragraph 12 of the statement, his first statement: "I want to emphasize that I did not personally see Vinko Pandurevic at standard that day." I'll skip a sentence or two. "I was only told that he was meeting with Vujadin Popovic and Beara. Also, I would not say that I knew Vujadin Popovic 'very well' as it says in the statement. I saw [sic] him by sight as the corps security officer from seeing him during my duties as a shoulder and MP. I also recognised him immediately on the ICTY wanted posters after the war." Now, Professor PW 165 has been entirely consistent in stating that although he was told Beara was present with Popovic in a meeting at the Zvornik brigade headquarters that he never saw or -- that Beara and Popovic, that he never saw Beara other than from the back. He never saw Beara's face, he says. Furthermore, he saw Popovic on TV as an accused. He saw Popovic on wanted posters and recognised him. Mr. Beara is on those same posters. Now, the first sentence of Rule 3 is: "The suspect and all others in the lineup must fit the description given by the witness at an earlier occasion." The last sentence of Rule 3 in your report: "Obviously, it is also useless to let the witness partake in a multiperson identity test when in fact the perpetrator, his face was never seen by the witness." And Rule 2, unconscious transference: "A lineup test would be invalid and should not be conducted if there's any chance that the witness may have seen the accused after the event." You said that very well yesterday at 25319. "One condition for a photo board photo board -- photo lineup testing it that it must be absolutely certain that there is no other possible place where the witness could have seen the accused apart from that one encounter at the scene of the crime as described in the indictment." So would it not - this man was interviewed in 2005 - been a gross violation of Rules 2 and 3 to conduct a lineup of this suspect when he says he's never seen the suspect's face and there's a very good chance that he saw the suspect's face after the encounter on a wanted poster for the same crime? So do you still maintain that there's no indication why it was impossible, undesirable, or unnecessary to test the claims of PW 165 in the situation described by him of seeing Beara only from the back?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, I think you've given me a number of very good arguments why it would be unwise to test this witness in a photo lineup. There are a few comments I would like to make. In the material I have received, the way I read it, it is not a hundred-percent clear that he consistently told he never saw Mr. Beara. In the statement I have in the witness testimony of the 26th of November, he says he probably never really saw Beara, which is not the same as I definitely never saw him. And also, at the transcript page 9962, he was told by some unknown person at the time of the alleged encounter that one of the persons he saw was Beara. That doesn't make it abundantly clear to me that actually he never saw anyone, and if you want to make sure whether he saw anyone, you might try an identification test. And, of course, you are quite right; you immediately run into the problem that then first you need a description of the person he saw, and that might be a good reason in the end not to do that. But it is not clear from the statement I have that it is attempted to the full to try to get a description of the person he saw. Even if he saw only a person from the back, that does not mean necessarily that you cannot do an identification attempt, only the photo board lineup should show peoples seen from the back. I've done that before, and there are sometimes in trials also witnesses who claim they could recognise a person from the back, which is not rejected as evidence in principle. It only means you cannot do an identification with faces. Another statement that you make is -- made is new for me, which is that the face of Mr. Beara was widely publicized through posters. I have he not seen those posters. I have not been made aware of these posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to show them to you in a little while.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But in general, of course, if Mr. Beara's face has been all over the country, then the same could be said about all witnesses, that they could have seen those pictures, which leads me to the general comment -- two general comments, which is if you do that as an investigation organisation, you should be aware that maybe that where you find witnesses, at the same time you have already destroyed the opportunities for testing their memories with respect to the outer appearance of the people wanted. And my second remark is that in view of these possibly widely publicized posters, it surprises me that some other witnesses were tested with videos and snapshots and so on because that then also would, of course, be totally meaningless.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You'll see, I think, that some of this depends on the timing of then those posters went out. Now, let me ask you this. I don't want to stay too long on this, but when the witness says, I only saw him from the back, and he's clear on that, the witness is adamant that I didn't see him, I didn't see him on cross-examination and which he's been consistent with, what kind of description are we going to get if we want to do a photo lineup of the face rather than the back of the head? How do we get a description if the witness says I didn't see him, which is required.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Sure, and I don't really want to oppose you, but I should point out a number of things. I'm not a finder of fact. I'm not to determine if there are statements by witnesses which change during the time. I'm not to determine which of those statements is the best representation of the truth. So my task is to look at, are there possible questions marks here, and could these question marks been resolved by further testing? That's all I do. If at cross-examination here in this Tribunal it finally is established by the finder of fact - but that's not me - that he actually never saw Mr. Beara, that's okay with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's not my question. The only thing I'm focusing on is your universe was the materials provided to you and your conclusions in your report, which in this case for this witness was that there was no indication why it was impossible, undesirable, or unnecessary, and that's what I am questioning you about. So the question of glasses, you make special mention that this witness did not describe glasses. You fault us for not doing a lineup for a witness who didn't describe glasses on a face he didn't see. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I would present it, but what I said in my table is - and I think I'm not misleading anyone by presenting it in this way - that this witness maybe saw Mr. Beara once from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. It's not even sure, and if he saw him, he saw him from behind. I think I made that abundantly clear in my table that that is the most he could have seen of him and possibly not, so I don't think there's any need to change, say, the way this witness was entered into my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Once you read that the witness stated that he had seen Popovic on wanted posters, you know, you said yesterday nothing was refused to you, did -- you know, knowing this is a genocide trial, the ICTY, you're familiar with the ICTY, the Srebrenica case, a big case, did you ask Mr. Ostojic or anybody on that team, hey, I need to know about whether your client was on wanted posters and, if so, the dates so I can match that up when tests were done or interviews were done?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I don't think I've been informed about those posters, and neither have I seen pictures of those posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, first of all, I don't want to testify, but we don't have a photograph of the back of Mr. Beara's head. But honestly, if that was a description we could get, which just what he looked like from the back, and we did a lineup of the backs of people's heads, and what -- and Mr. Ostojic called you, what probative value what would you say that identification had? Even if he picked out the correct back of the head, would that be an identification?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The value of that identification if done with the back of the heads would at least be as good as any other identification, and if the witness would have been given, say, a fair lineup and the proper instructions which discouraged him from guessing, in my universe, as you call it, that would be significant evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you ever testified in any of the thousand trials you testified in -- well, first of all, was there ever a lineup of the backs of heads presented to Court and have you ever -- second question is have you testified, yeah, that's a fair lineup, that's a good idea of the defendant?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have seen the strangest lineups of people with Mickey Mouse masks on because that's what the suspect saw. The only thing you try to do in a lineup is present the accused in exactly the way he was seen by witnesses, and you make sure the foils in the lineup match that description. So it could be that the witness is asked to recognise the build or the gait of a person with a Mickey Mouse mask on, so anything can be used, and sometimes that is successful. There's no particular reason why the back of the head would be -- should be excluded from lineups, although, we know, of course, that it's easier to recognise a person by the face than by the back. But if witnesses claim they have seen only the back and later claim they recognise someone by the back of his head, then there's a good reason to test that, just in the same manner as which happens quite regularly, that people claim to recognise the posture of a person or the build or the way he walks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question was, though - thank you - is has that ever happened in any of the thousand trials you testified at, that the Prosecutor's presented a lineup of backs of heads and it's been used and you've said that's okay? Has that ever actually happened? I'm not talking about hypotheticals.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. No, with the back of the head has not happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But with the heads covered, with fake moustaches, Mickey Mouse mask. Anything can be done. There's no particular reason why lineups should be restricted to the typical facial photographs that you usually see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, given I've informed you about the wanted posters and I've -- and we've discussed the -- what the witness saw with a little more depth, do you still maintain that there's no indication why it was impossible, undesirable, or unnecessary to do a lineup test for PW 165, or do you think that there might be reasons not to?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the case is if the lineup -- if the posters show the face, which he claims he'd never seen, anyway, because he says I saw -- maybe saw the back, then showing the face of Mr. Beara on posters would not be a reason not to test his ability to recognise the back of a person because seeing the face would not be helpful in that lineup at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But we couldn't do a face lineup is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't do that face lineup. You couldn't do that, anyway, if he never saw that face.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Okay. Now, we have agreed and you explained quite well yesterday in a question about using video stills to make photo boards, you need a reasonably good quality of the suspect to make a fair, probative photo board, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to bring -- first of all, here's for more information than context for you. Up until March of 1997, we did not have photos of Mr. Beara, and I'll show you the photo we've had, which I think you've seen, 65 ter 1983. And I shouldn't say photos; I should say images because the first thing we got was the video clip, which you've seen, I'll show you a still from that. Now, our position is that Mr. Beara is the gentleman on the left with the glasses and no hat. Clearly, that still is not suitable for a lineup, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next -- I want to show you 3656 now, please. This is a passport photo of Mr. Beara, which we got on September 2002. So until September 2002 all we had was that still, and then we got this photo. That's a reasonable photo for a lineup, I take it, or you tell me. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quality of that photo is better, but there's one problem, which is that in this photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see, yeah.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- his appearance might have changed compared to what witnesses might have seen in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, because it's --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the problem is that preferably, of course, you would have a good photograph, not a recent photograph, but a photograph representing the accused's appearance in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly, because this is seven years later. 3636, please. This is one you've seen. This is the next and third image we get of Beara in fall 2005, and so I just wanted to show you this is what we had at various times.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This would be a very good picture, I think, because I estimate it that it comes from about that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During the war, clearly.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: During -- yeah, I can't say that, but it's suggestive of war conditions, and I think that the face is clearly enough to be used in a photo lineup. There's nothing wrong about the cap. It only means that the foils also should wear caps, but that's done before by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you want to use the entire picture in order, also, to show his build, then the only thing you need to do is remove the insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could we go -- which, actually, I'll do that now. You made a slight error in your testimony yesterday. You said that one of the problems in showing this photo to Erdemovic was insignia, but in fact - and I think my friend will agree with me; it's in the stipulation - the insignia were blacked out in the photos shown to Mr. Erdemovic. That's just for your information. Okay. Now, I want to talk to you about those wanted posters that I referenced, that I think we agreed if a witness had seen a wanted poster with Mr. Beara's face on it subsequent to the incident but before the test it would invalidate the test because of possible unconscious transference or conscious transference.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It would invalidate a test that makes use of faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Let's go through these, if I can, and let me give you some dates first that are I think beyond dispute. 21st of October, 2002, is when Mr. Beara's indictment was unsealed, and that means made public. Everybody in the world knows about it, can read about it. 10th of October, 2004, is when Mr. Beara was taken into custody in The Hague. So that is also the time frame you'll see of the wanted posters because he is not on posters before the indictment is unsealed, obviously, and once he has been arrested then there's no need to keep putting him on further printings of the posters, although old posters may still be around. And could we bring up 65 ter 3637, please. This is a series of wanted posters. I'll run through them quickly. If you need to see the hard copy, if it's too small, I'll give you one, Professor. This first one -- that's fine. We can see the date 30th, October 2002, meaning a few days, ten days after the indictment was unsealed, and you'll see that Mr. Beara is the first person on the poster because of the spelling of his name. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to the next page. The next printing. A little bit bigger, please. Thank you. 20th of January, 2003, it's the same, and you may notice, too, that the photo of Mr. Beara is the same one as the passport photo that we received at just about that same time.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Next one, please. Thank you. And if we could just scroll down to the bottom because the date's on the bottom for some reason. 15 of August 2003. This is all while the window between the unsealing of the indictment and the arrest. Next one, please. Maybe we have -- oh, I missed one. We don't need to go -- no, this is right. I'm sorry. This is 26 November 2003 if we look at the bottom, and there's only two more, which we can just scroll through quickly, which are 10th March, 2004, and 19 July 2004. If we just click through those. So just to save time, I won't comment on those, but what we've seen are -- during this window, which I've outlined, five separate printings of this photo where Beara is always the first one. Now, if we could have 65 ter 3645, please. I got to say the redactions are just the names in the field offices. I can show that to my friend if he wants to see them, but we just redacted the names. This is just an example, a distribution of the -- one of the posters showing the printing and how many were sent out, and we can see at the bottom how many there were, 1135 in English, 85 in French, 495 in Cyrillic, and the different places where these were distributed, and the second page is similar. Now, you may not have been to the region, but I think we can agree that the point of a wanted poster is to be seen by people, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. So these are widely distributed in the areas Zvornik, Bratunac, post offices, police stations, municipality buildings, all boarder crosses between Zvornik and Serbia where many of our witnesses have testified they crossed frequently, offices of international organizations, billboards sometimes, and they were also all over the internet, but they're prevalent where our witnesses live. Let me show you a 65 ter 3664, if I can. Turn that around. In addition, Interpol has posters for him. I'm not sure how useful that particular one would be. For -- not for us, for other reasons, so he's also on other posters, and I'm showing you these. You agree -- well, let me continue, and then I'll ask you the question because I want to go through the media and the press. Can we look at 3643, please, and let me just ask you this before we look at these. Did you ask or inquire of the Beara Defence about images of Beara that may have been in the local press in the former Yugoslavia or on the internet at the time that some of these interviews you were analyzing were being conducted? Did you ask about that kind of image distribution?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed possible images that could have been seen. I did not ask specifically for posters because I was unaware that he ever appeared on a poster.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is just a sample I'll show you of --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is the 20th of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, 20th of October, 2004, and you remember Mr. Babic. Mr. 165 we just talked about was interviewed in 2005 for the first time. If we go to 3644, please. That's 14 October 2004. I'll be asking you some more questions about that photo a little later. About Mr. -- this article, I don't have a translation, but it's about Mr. Beara being transferred to this Tribunal after his arrest. 3668. And this is Vreme, a local paper. Glas-javnosti, another one, 14 October 2004. And I'm not going to -- let's skip to 3670, if we can, to save time. 12 October 2004, same passport photo. This one in English just to show that it's also in the international press. 3671. Wanted persons from the poster are also shown on -- you can see here on international websites, this one from the US Department of State. We can skip 3672. We can skip 3673 just to save time. Now, you've acknowledged this problem of witnesses possibly seeing the image or the person afterwards in your report - that was with Witness PW 162 and Peric - and you say that lineups wouldn't be appropriate for these witnesses because they said they may have seen Beara on TV or in the press. Now that you've seen that distribution of images, press, internet, TV, and physically placed wanted posters, that would also be true for anybody interviewed in your table who was interviewed after those -- after that distribution of his image, correct? They shouldn't be tested?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, exactly the same reasoning applies to all witnesses who might have seen pictures of Mr. Beara. In the awareness that such pictures have been distributed, it would of course have been also necessary to always ask witnesses whether they have seen those pictures or not. I saw those references in two of the statements where it was asked, and they said, yes, indeed, I have. The reason why I did not group other witnesses with the two you mentioned, PW 162 and Peric, is that such statements I did not find in the files of the other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, though --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But logically, of course, you are completely correct. If they were interviewed after the publication of these witnesses, they should have been asked about seeing these witnesses, and if there is even a slight possibility even if they had not been aware of it, that they could have seen them, that would make it -- that would be a good reason not to submit him to further tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm looking at your Rule 2 from your report, which is on page 4, and you -- and that's what I call the after rule, can't have seen the witness after the encounter. And here's what you say there: "If there has been such an extra exposure to the outer appearance of the suspect, a lineup test would be invalid and should, therefore, not be conducted. It does not matter whether the witness testifies that he was not influenced by this encounter or that he did not pay attention during this other encounter" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. -- "that he does not remember this other encounter or that he did not even recognise the suspect at this other encounter because it is unconscious." So -- and as I said, Professor, I was in Limaj for your testimony, and I paid attention, and what I got from it is if you got a witness from a place like Zvornik or Bratunac, when I go there there's wanted posters everywhere, I would say -- or you tell me. Doesn't matter if the witness says, I've never seen a wanted poster. It's -- what could be more dangerous than seeing the photo of the person on a wanted poster even if you don't remember it or -- I mean, isn't that just a flat-out reason why you should not test a person if there's the possibility, a reasonable possibility that they saw that poster?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely. We don't have to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clearly stated in my report. There's no reason to change that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that will shorten some of my cross. I'm going to go to Rajko Babic, another witness in your table. He's the second in your table. This is a -- he testified here on 18 of April, 2007, interviewed for the first time in September 2005 when Mr. Beara was already in custody. And he had a face-to-face discussion with a lieutenant-colonel - that's at TR10237 to 10240 - in broad daylight. So in principle, no observation problems there, correct? Face-to-face discussion during daytime?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he gives a description at -- I won't bother reading it at 10240. It's not in your report, I don't think, but in 65 ter 2D0011, page 5, paragraph 8, he also -- which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- which was provided to you, he also described the colonel in his 50s. Now, in your report you talk about the photos shown to Mr. Babic. This is on page 10 of your report --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- in the second paragraph. And you say, It's even more surprising as none of -- as they contained no image of Mr. Beara, all the photos shown to Mr. Babic, but now the discussion we've just had about the exposure this witness to Bratunac might have had to Mr. Beara's image as an ICTY accused, now that you know that, it's not surprising, is it, that the investigators didn't show him images of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to me it was surprising that in an interrogation about Mr. Beara where you show pictures and ask whether he recognised someone, you show him pictures where he could not possibly recognise Mr. Beara because he was not in the pictures. If it's meant as a test to see whether he would make a false positive, then in principle that could have been arranged in such a way, although that's not a usual thing to do and could also be considered a somewhat misleading way of teaching witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't think that was the intention. So I really do not understand what the meaning was of showing these pictures. That was why I was surprised to see that it had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, but let me say, you're an expert in your field, but you are not a criminal investigator.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I don't mean that to be flippant, but that's not your expertise, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I put it to you that there are reasons to show witnesses photo, lots of photos of other people, not to identify so -- just to get leads. Can you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the investigators very well with the witness may say, all right, we're going to show you a bunch of photos. Just tell us if you see any of these people regardless of whether they are meant to be indicted or not or a suspect, but just who are they, do you know them, and purposefully remove the photo for Mr. Beara so they don't say, oh, I know that guy, and then you would come in and say, well, that's -- that doesn't mean anything, that's an inappropriate identification --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, although some comment can be made about that method of investigation. If you show photographs of people to witnesses to find out whether they can give you a lead, at the same time that means, as you already suggest, that these witnesses cannot be used later on to identify those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm always surprised if I say how easily and how quickly during early investigation stages photographs are shown to witnesses without the realization that that way you lost the witnesses for later identification purposes, which is not a problem if you have lots and lots of witnesses, but which can be very problematic if there is a scarcity of witnesses. And that is why I always recommend that you show photographs to witnesses in order to find a lead if you are desperate because there's no other way of getting leads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But there --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that practice of showing photographs to get a lead in the investigation is a technique that really surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Because, see, what we need to do is find people and interview them to get more information; and occasionally, Professor, can you see that it might be worthwhile showing photos to generate those leads, to get information even if we accept we'll never be able to do a photo lineup of this person with the individual who pointed him out to us. Is that reasonable?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That situation can happen, and I'm not an investigator, as you said. But as an expert I've seen numerous cases where later on it was realized that there weren't -- were not so many witnesses and that it was still attempted to do identifications with witnesses who provided leads on the basis of photographs. And that's why -- and also in my publications I sometimes warned against that practice explaining that you should do that only if you have many witnesses and you can easily lose a few or if you are desperate. In one of my publications out of 2005, I spent a whole chapter to that problem where in the robbery of a station office in their other station, all suspects were first shown photographs to get a lead, and that way they lost six witnesses and had no witnesses left for a conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to correct the record, a small -- I think small mistake you made yesterday in your testimony at 25333 discussing Mr. Babic. You talked about how showing the pictures to Mr. Babic meant that he could not be tested in a photo lineup anymore, and then you said that he did not recognise anyone in the pictures because whether he should have recognised Mr. Beara in these pictures if he really met him, it all also depends on the quality of the pictures, implying that Mr. Beara was included in those pictures, but I just want to point out to you that --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- that he was not. Your report is correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I think we can agree now, just to keep it straight, that there were reasons not to do a photo lineup of Mr. Babic considering his exposure to the images of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was, and I can't see that in my report, if the first time he was interrogated after the publication of these photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, September 2005, so we can agree. We can agree he shouldn't have been tested with a lineup?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm moving on now to Mr. Boering. He's a -- Major Boering, the fourth witness on your table, and as you state there in your Column 3, here there are two encounters, twice, and you've got it just right, first in dusk for 15 to 30 minutes, and the second during lunch for 30 to 60 minutes. And that second meeting you'll see was at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. You refer in para 2 of Section 2 -- or Section 2 of Section 2 of your report, the poor lighting conditions. Now, I took that to mean you were talking about the first encounter that Major Boering had with who we say was Mr. Beara, correct? Because I didn't see anywhere else where there were poor lighting conditions, but you correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've described lighting conditions in general. It's a general factor that should always be considered. It's not limited to this witnesses -- to this particular witness. You should ask about all witnesses, what were the lighting conditions? I'm not quite certain - I should just review all the cases - whether Mr. Boering is the only one who described poor lighting conditions, but my statement in the report is a general statement about lighting conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see. All right. Well, you don't need to stop now and do that, but if you think of any of the others -- here, we describe dusk, so that's what I thought you were referring to. Still, even at dusk a 15- to 30-minute face-to-face conversation is not bad for exposure time, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I never said that lighting conditions are an absolute obstacle to seeing faces, but if there is a question about how well could he see him, and lighting conditions might be one reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then the answer to that question can be obtained from an identification test.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And the second one, I think we'll agree, the second meeting, lunchtime, 30 to 60 minutes, daylight, no observation problems there?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'll try to shorten this, but I want to quickly go through these two encounters. The first one according to Major Boering's testimony is sometime in March or April 1995. He describes this at page 5 of his 1998 statement, which is 4000025, and he says that Momir Nikolic introduced me to a VRS officer named Colonel Beara, and then he describes their conversation. In the same statement at page 6, he talks about one month later approximately after that first meeting, he again meets with Momir Nikolic and Colonel Beara, this time at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac for lunch, and they discuss the same topic at both meetings, the problem of Naser Oric. And I won't go through it, but there's a lot of description in there about their lunch and their conversation at both. Now, let me just read you a little bit of the cross-examination of Major Boering that was conducted by counsel for Mr. Beara by his Defence. He is asking Boering about this lunch. This is at 2109 in the transcript: "Okay. And let me refresh your recollection if I can. Do you recall that on that meeting it was a luncheon meeting and that you had food, and you had drinks, you had meat, lamb, and fish. Do you remember that?" And then Major Boering continues on: "I'm not sure I remember exactly what we ate. "Question: Do you recall that it was a luncheon-type meeting where you met Mr. Beara at the Hotel Fontana, sir? "Answer: Yes. "Question: Do you remember there were two black soldiers there that were going to sit at another table until Mr. Beara said, no, come sit with us, and you put a separate table at the end so the black soldiers could sit with you and eat lunch?" And then Mr. Meeks continues to ask Mr. Beara at 2111 about the conversation regarding Naser Oric. So from that material provided to you, it's clear that Defence counsel for Mr. Beara do not contest the lunch meeting with Mr. Beara. They have accepted that; he is there; it is their case that he is at that second meeting. That's clear from the transcript, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I should make conclusions about that because it's something I should conclude, right? It's not something I can read in the transcript. It's not Defence counsel saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we do not contest that ourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, he is. He says, let me remind you what you had for lunch here and who you ate with, the witness says, well, I remember this, I remember that. They are both agreeing about this lunch, but I'll move on if you feel you can't --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But to my mind, it also could mean, let me remind you to what you told about it without the explicit statement of Defence that they agreed that is the truth, so it's not for me to determine whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in truth the Defence already conceded that this meeting had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about in truth. I'm talking about as the fact pattern of --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- the science of whether tests should be --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what the logical implication is of what you because you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can see where I'm going?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't think I should make logical conclusions. That's not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll -- just a couple of things. This is the cross-examination of Major Boering about the first meeting, the prior meeting. Mr. Meeks: "I want to talk to you briefly about your alleged meeting, first meeting with Mr. Beara."

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the dusk?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, as in 2117.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Clear they contest that meeting. And then later on, 2117, Mr. Meeks says: "I want to know, do you have a specific recollection of who it was that contacted you about this purported meeting?" And later at 2121, Mr. Meeks says: "What was the subject specifically of this conversation you purportedly had at Checkpoint Jovo, first meeting with Mr. Beara?" So Rule 2, it seems quite simple to me. We just talked about it. If there has been such an extra exposure to the outer appearance of the suspect, a lineup test would be invalid, and therefore, it should not be conducted, a second exposure. Now, just as a -- we'll make it a hypothetical, if all parties agree that Mr. Beara and Major Boering were at the second meeting, a lineup test wouldn't tell us anything about the first meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you accept that hypothesis, which is not mine, then a positive identification, it only means he knows that person, and you can only interpret that as having met at a certain occasion if there's only one possible occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the logic of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And here we've got these -- under my fact pattern, we'll -- he should not -- so if my hypothesis is correct, then Major Boering, as well, should not have been tested in a formal lineup, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move to Mr. Egbers, the fourth one on your witness table, and his statements and testimony, which you've read. He talks about first a meeting, Major Zoran Malinic, and the transcript's provided to you at TR2670. Mr. Egbers testified about how he was told by Malinic that Malinic needed to contact Colonel Beara to solve the problem, and he testifies that the next day Colonel Beara arrived, and Egbers testifies that he spoke with him. Now, I'd like to bring up 65 ter number 2D00024. I'd like to go to page 6. Well, page 1 first, excuse me. All right. We can see here this is a Royal Netherlands Army Srebrenica debriefing, and that's not what I'm most interested in. What I'm interested in is the attachment to that meeting, which is at page 6, the report which is attached.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. What's the date of this debriefing? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think this one, Professor, unfortunately is undated, but the document I'm going to show you does have a date. On page 6, this is a report which Egbers drafted on the 15th of July, 1995, which according to him was the day after he met with Colonel Beara at Nova Kasaba, and he describes this encounter at paragraphs 8 to 10. "As a large group of BiH fighters was assembling, several BSA units advanced." And that is how they wrote the Bosnian-Serb army at that time, the VRS. "Our safety could not be guaranteed because Major Zoran had no contact with them. His commanding officer Colonel Beara would look into the matter." Paragraph 9: "I made the acquaintance of the Colonel. He wore the insignia of his rank and drove an expensive car." Paragraph 10: "I gave an account of what happened to us, which was written down. Colonel Beara has the original, and there was a copy in the possession of Section 2/3." Now, that doesn't have a description of Colonel Beara, but we talked a bit earlier about refreshing and remembering names, and that's a perfect way to refresh or remember a name, isn't it, to write the name down very soon after the incident or after you learn it, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I would not even call it refreshing. This is committing it to memory. When you write down, it is committed to memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, Egbers testified here in October 2006, and he described his meeting with Colonel Beara, a person introduced to him as Colonel Beara at Nova Kasaba. And he says this: "Question" -- reading his report -- "Now, it proceeds to say I contacted Colonel Beara in the morning. Do you see that? "Answer: Yes. "Question: How did you make contact with him? Did you call him? "Answer: He got out of his car. I went to him. I even saluted him, and I told him who I was, and he told me who he was. He didn't say much, but that's, I think, the answer to your question." A little bit further down, this is on page 2821: "I walked towards him, and I saluted him, and then he saluted me back. "Question: Now, in the statement it never states that Mr. Beara ever introduced himself to you. He goes on the next four lines to state the interpreter told me his name. Do you see that? "Answer: That's correct."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise again. "Question: Is it your recollection now that he introduced himself to you? "Answer: Well, I told my name to him and explained who I was, and he didn't speak English very well that time, but he mentioned his name, and the interpreter, he translated everything in English to me, and he told me that he was Colonel Beara." And then he goes on to say this was around 10 to 15 minutes outside the school. So I think we can agree no observation problems there, face-to-face, short conversation in daylight.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And no problems what the name we just said writing it down. And could we have 65 ter number 2D00019 up, please. This is from a 24 October 1995 [Realtime transcript read in error, "2005"] ICTY statement. If we could go to page 7, please, of the English.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said 2005. I saw on the page 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's -- I'm sorry. Yeah, it's 1995. I don't know if I said it wrong or it was the transcript, but you're correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript says 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, it's 1995.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. And again, in this statement made in 1995, Egbers writes: "On Friday, 14 July 1995, I contacted Colonel Beara in the morning. I spoke to him. He read the statement, and nothing was discussed. This man wore badges denoting that he was a colonel. He wore a camouflage uniform. He was 45 to 50 years old. He was about 1.9 metres tall. His hair was grey. I saw that he drove in a luxurious car. I believe it was an Opel Omega. The interpreter told me his name." So he's told that the person that's going to resolve the situation is Colonel Beara. He is expecting to meet Colonel Beara. The next day, he meets Colonel Beara, has a short conversation. The day after that or that night, he writes down the name Colonel Beara. And in October 1995, he gives a description. That's all - isn't it - at the beginning a decent way of - you tell me - processing and beginning to retain a memory of meeting a person?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conditions as they are described in this document allow an adequate representation of things in memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question before the break, just to remind you, at that point we didn't have a photo at all of Mr. Beara, so you agree with me, it's plain common sense, we can't do a photo lineup without a decent photo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, when this statement was taken.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is so that you didn't have a photograph at that moment, but I'm not -- I cannot verify that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But if you accept that we were not at fault?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have not a photograph, you cannot do a lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. We'll have a 25-minute break. How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can try to speed up, but I hope I can finish in the next session, Judge. I'm going to proceed in the same way. I have specific questions about specific witnesses that I think I need to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to know how long. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Agius had to leave us due to an urgent personal matter. We will be sitting pursuant to 15 bis. Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Professor, I apologise. I'm going to go back and ask you a question about number 2 on your table, Mr. Babic, which I had forgotten to ask you. Now, before I do that, the summaries that we talked about, 3696, were those -- who actually typed those up? Was that physically typed up by you? I'm talking about the summaries now, not the table, or was that typed up by the Defence when they were working with you?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, these were typed up by the Defence when they were working -- I think when I was working with Mr. Philip De Man. At least it was produced on their machine, not my machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can look at your table in your report - for the record again, 2D574, page 9, that is - for Mr. Babic who we discussed earlier in the third column, "saw him how," you've written, "Probably never." Now, isn't that doing exactly what you said was not your role, deciding on whether the witness did or did not in reality actually see Mr. Beara? Isn't that the Trial Chamber's job?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, you are correct. I should have said that there is a question mark about whom he saw and how he saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that and -- because I think we can agree, of course, you have no idea --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is my wording, as you see in my original notes, the handwritten notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I accept that. I accept that. But you have no idea whether Mr. Babic met with or saw Beara that day on the 15th July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I have no opinion who ever met anyone at all in this case. I only discuss how it could have been tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Back, now, to Mr. Egbers, I still want to look at your table here. Again, Column 3, "saw him how," and with all the statements, transcripts, some of which we've covered and many more that were available to you, you've written, "saw him how," "once, was introduced to him, did not pay much attention." And you, again, said yesterday in your testimony at transcript 25322 that Egbers said that he did not pay much attention at this meeting. Now -- and the last paragraph of your report, you say that Egbers denied seeing Beara wear glasses. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but the total of the analysis in your report which you've provided to the Trial Chamber about Egbers is those two things I've read out to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I quote in my report what I guess is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what you say, that of course does not mean that I pretend to have given there a complete representation of Egbers' statements. It's only -- the table is meant as a reminder for the Court, but of course I am aware that the Court has read all Egbers' statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, if we could look at 65 ter 3696 at page 10. That is the summary for Mr. Egbers and, again, we should only broadcast page 10, not the first page. There we have the citation to this portion of your report. It's a little bit down on the first section: "Witness allegedly met and spoke to Beara in a parking place. He didn't pay much attention to the appearance of the person he had allegedly seen." And we see the transcript reference at page 2824, line 16. Now, what I want to do is read out a bit of that transcript page where line 16 comes in. This was on cross-examination. "Question: Right. How about eyewear, sir? When you describe someone, would you say someone if they wear glasses, wouldn't you describe them by saying they wear glasses, or if you don't mention glasses, can I presume that Mr. Beara on 14 July 1995 was not wearing glasses given your immediately recent testimony? If you saw, you would have written it down, et cetera, if he had it. "Answer: Well, I haven't wrote that down. I don't recall whether he wears glasses. He did wear glasses at that time, but I didn't write it up. He stepped out of a car. I don't know whether he had glasses or not." "Question: How about facial features like eyes, the shape of his eyes, the colour of his eyes? Do you recall that at all?" "Answer: Well, I've got to explain the situation. We were there with 12 Dutch peacekeepers. There were -- there were terrible things going on. We were concerned about the safety of us and all the others in the surroundings. The one who was in charge of -- was capable to get us back was this Colonel Beara. That's what they told me. That's what this major told me and the translator told me. And when I met him, I was only focusing on getting the things done I wanted to be done, so I didn't focus on the colour of his eyes. There are a lot of impressions -- other impressions at that day, of course, as you can imagine. So instead of going to all these facial remarks or his eyes, did he have a scar or not, it's just a minor detail in my story. Of course, for you it's an important one, but I've described him as I described him as being a tall, 1.90 metres, a colonel of the Bosnian/Serb army, who came out of a car, a luxurious car, who I saluted, who saluted back. We talked about it. This was the Colonel Beara, the interpreter said. This is what I remember." Now, from that answer, the only information you provide the Court citing here for your analysis is that Egbers "did not pay much attention." Is that fair? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not -- what I say is not a total representation of Egbers' experiences on that particular day. It's the essential thing when it comes to Egbers' storing information about the outer appearance of the person he met, and to me, my discipline, it's essential to say he states he did not pay much attention because the whole perception and memory process as I explained the other day starts with paying attention. When you don't pay attention there it stops, so to me, that's a crucial piece of information. And I never pretended that my table is a complete representation of Egbers testimony. There's no way it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but my point is this, Professor. He doesn't say anywhere here that he didn't pay attention. I think a fair reading of this is that all of his attention was focused on this Beara who he saw as his only way out of this difficult situation. He says he didn't pay attention to whether he was wearing glasses or the shape or colour of his eyes. He doesn't say he wasn't paying attention during this encounter, does he?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's saying he does not pay much attention to his outer appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where does he say that? He says he described him, 1.9, a colonel.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but not to facial marks. He says remarks, but it's facial marks and his ability to identify him later so that we can be a little bit more certain about who he met. It's probably not based on the length of person because the length of a person is not such a unique descriptor that you may recognise someone on the basis of that. For me, for recognition, say, the most relevant thing would be, the most useful thing would be if he had stored the face itself, but he says he did not, which - and let me be clear about that - does not mean that he does not remember the face. To me, it means there is some uncertainty there because he said that he paid attention to other things and that uncertainty can be removed by a test. That's the only thing I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also said in your report he denied that Beara wore glasses, and you made a distinction yesterday between witnesses who don't remember glasses and witness who deny. But your report's not quite accurate on that point, correct? He says here he doesn't remember, not that he denies.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not remember wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. But my point is that in your report you state that he -- that Egbers said is one of the people who denied that.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me check this because in my summary statement, it states correctly, witness does not remember if Beara was wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what my summary statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me check in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the last sentence of your report, it says: "For Witnesses 135 and number 21, the denial of having seen any glasses constitutes all the more reasons why they should have been tested." And Egbers is number 21 in your table.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. You're right, but it should read the denial of remembering any glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now, the fact -- now, you talked on your direct examination about the showing of the video to Egbers, and you stated, and I agree, that according to your rules, showing that video is not a proper lineup. However, the fact that that video is not a proper lineup doesn't in any way diminish his recollection of the event and his testimony. If he sees a video and says however many times he watches it, yeah, that's Colonel Beara, the fact that that wasn't a proper test doesn't detract in any way from his testimony and his statements, does it? It just means the test isn't valid?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you're asking me. I'm not denying that he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Know what? That was a bad question. I'm sorry. My point is, in the situation with Mr. Egbers in 2000, I believe it was, he was shown that video after he has made various statements and all of this, the fact that that video was shown to him and was an improper test means that the test isn't valid as an identification, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But it doesn't detract from his statements and his testimony about what he saw and remembered? You can't say, because the test wasn't performed properly, you should discount anything from his testimony.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He said what he said before he was shown the video, so the video could not have affected what he said. That's a logical point. But after he was shown a video, there is, of course, a problem because what he says further can be influenced by seeing the video, probably not on the events of that particular day, but if later on he describes the person he saw again, that description might be affected by seeing the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But the video, the description I showed you from 1995, of course, that's not affected negatively in any way, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that came before seeing the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Let's go now -- and again, you have no criticism of his memory of the name and rank of the Colonel Beara that he met and wrote down the next day, as a memory expert?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although, of course, I'm not aware of the particular circumstances in which he did that, but I did not report on that aspect of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, number 151 out of your table, Erdemovic, Witness number 151. He's number 8 on your table. I'm not going to go over this in detail because it's the subject of stipulations which have been filed, and those are agreements between the parties. I just want to correct one point in your report for the record. A mistake, I believe, was made there. You state in paragraph 3 of Section 2 of your report that the presentation of photographs -- let me just check that, sorry. Yeah, sorry, that's right. Page 10, paragraph 3. "The presentation of photographs to Witnesses 122 and 151" - 151 is Erdemovic - "was even more surprising as they contain no image of Mr. Beara." Now, we don't need to bring the photo up again, but I think you'll agree with me, that's a mistake. He was phone a photo of Mr. Beara, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was shown -- he was also shown a photo, and that's where this comment came from on which Mr. Beara was not present. He was also shown a --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but some photos contain pictures of -- at least that's what I've been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. So -- and shown in the stipulation which was provided to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And so that sentence of the report needs to be corrected because he was shown an image of Mr. Beara. It says he was not in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but he was also shown an image without Mr. Beara. He was shown several photos. One of these photos --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was what I know came from the Krstic exhibit 28/15, which did not contain a picture of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is reading the plain language of your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. You're right. That could be misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how did that happen? I mean, do you know how you got that wrong or how that came in?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say it's wrong, but that's the way you read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me read it again. "The presentation of photographs to Witnesses 122 and 151" - Erdemovic, that is - "was even more surprising as they contained no image of Mr. Beara." Now, the way I read that is that all the photographs shown to him contained no image of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it should read: "As some of them contained no image of Mr. Beara." That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Could I have 3704 up, please. I'll skip that. That's all right. Before we get to the next witness, let me ask you about something you said in the Limaj trial. This was at 7151 to 7152. You were asked a question and you answered -- or you stated -- sorry, let me strike that. 7157 to 7158. That's 65 ter number 3666 in e-court. And you were asked this question: "Question: The point I'm trying to ask you about with this study is the effect of increased exposure time on accuracy of indications" -- "of identifications." And as I say, that should be page 7157 in e-court, so we need to go ahead ten pages -- one page, sorry. "And its fair to say all things being equal, an increase in exposure time is going to lead to -- is -- correlates with increased accuracy in identification. Is that a statement you would agree with?" And you answered: "Yeah, there's no doubt about it." "Question" - it's not really a question - "Okay." Then on page 7158, you say: "If you would have asked me what's the minimum exposure that you do need, I would say 300 milliseconds. Above that, it becomes quite good." Now, do you stand -- is that correct still today?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you now about Witness 126, Milosevic. This concerns a 14 July encounter. He's number 10 on your table. He was interviewed in 2002 and testified here in June 2007. Now, this is the witness, you may remember, who was ordered by his commander to deliver a message to Colonel Beara at the school, and he testified at TR1302: "And later in the day, did you receive some instructions from your commander? "Answer: Well, yes. Sometime in the afternoon, he was also called from the brigade, or at least that's what he told me, and he asked me to look for Mr. Beara near the elementary school and to convey a message to him to report to the brigade command, and this is exactly what I did." Now, thinking here about refreshing and names, if you have to deliver a message to somebody who you don't know or haven't met named Beara, then you have to remember that name, perhaps even refresh it as you go along to do the task you were ordered, correct, so the process of imprinting that name Beara would begin even before the encounter?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one possibility, and I really am not to judge that exact situation. It's also possible that he would be sent and saying, go there and there, there is the colonel, tell him this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but if we accept his testimony that he was told to look for Mr. Beara, then he needs to remember that name in order to deliver it to the correct person. I mean, if you tell me, you've got to find my student Ms. So-and-so in Leiden and give her a copy of the report, I need to remember that name when I'm going to Leiden, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. That's why I try to explain. You need to know a lot more about the situation. If I'm told, you will be examined by the Prosecutor Mr. Nicholls, well, there's one person examining me, so I don't need to know your name. I just assume that's Mr. Nicholls, and I don't have to remember the name.
