If I'm told, go there and there in that office, Ms. So-and-so will give you something, if there's only one person in the office, I need especially to remember where the office is and not what the name of Ms. So-and-so is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it depends on the situation. If this person is sent to a certain place where someone is in charge, he needs to find a person in charge as it goes in the army, and if there's someone else who's the highest rank, you go to that person. In his recollection later on, but that's already -- that's why I'm saying this, the danger is that he's now reconstructing that he was sent to meet certain Mr. Beara, whereas in fact he was just looking for the highest in rank or the only colonel. So I don't know exactly what's going on in his mind, and in order to make any -- from a scientific point of view -- and in that respect my discipline is different from yours, from a scientific point of view, this is not sufficient for me to make a fair interpretation of what probably has gone on in his -- what probably was conveyed into his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But if from your scientific discipline, if we accept that what he says he remembers that he was told to look for Mr. Beara and there were several people at the scene when he arrives, normally if you were asked to deliver a message to somebody where there may be several people you need to remember -- you don't want to show up and say, does somebody want this? I mean, you need to remember who you're taking it to. That's basic. Forget about this situation.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be logical for a finder of fact. This is not a scientific fact I can confirm for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this witness knew, was familiar with the accused Drago Nikolic who is in this trial. He is sitting next to Mr. Beara, and according to this witness's testimony, when he arrives at the school Colonel [sic] Drago Nikolic, who he knows, points out Beara to the witness as the person he needs to talk to. And the witness then speaks face-to-face, he says, with Mr. Beara for two or three minutes. No exposure problem there. This is daylight, two- to three-minute conversation, face to face, correct, if that's the way it occurred?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Two to three minutes face-to-face conversation is adequate exposure time?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for record, line 3, I take it Nikolic is not a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's my mistake if I said that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that is an important detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Let me read what the witness actually said. This is at TR1303 to 1304. "I went to the school" -- and this was provided to you. "I went to the school, and since I did not know Beara, I had learned the name for the first time. At the crossroads of the roads leading to the school, I came across Drago Nikolic, and since I had been his assistant, i.e., his security officer in his battalion, we had known each other. I asked him whether anybody by the name of Beara was there, and he pointed a person to me. I approached the man. We greeted each other, and I conveyed the message to him, and the message was that he should contact the brigade. And after that I returned to the battalion, and I briefed my commander, Ostoja Stanisic, as to what had happened. In other words, I was a courier on that occasion, and having done what I did my mission was accomplished." And I don't need to read any more where he describes where this took place. He also described this similarly in his testimony in Blagojevic. I don't know if you were given that. I don't remember. That's 3665, and there he says: "I addressed Drago Nikolic, and he told me that this was, indeed, Beara." So my question is, if we accept this testimony under this fact pattern, without observation problems we've agreed, the witness has had a good opportunity to imprint and remember the name Beara. He's looking for Beara. He's introduced to Beara.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say good. You asked me would that be sufficient. That would be sufficient. That doesn't mean it's also guaranteed. So if -- where any party in this trial it is challenged that he actually saw Mr. Beara or challenged that he stored an adequate image of the person he saw, then two to three minutes is also short enough to say there might be some doubt in two to three minutes. That's not a lifetime. And so to resolve that question, that's whole point of my report, I think. If there is such a question, and I'm not saying there is such a question, but if there is such a question about whom he actually met, one way to get better information about it is a lineup test.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Drago Nikolic's attorneys did not challenge this encounter - it's at TR13345 - and asked the witness simply to mark where this took place and asked him questions. You've seen security officer Momir Nikolic introduce Beara to Boering. Here we have security officer Drago Nikolic introducing Beara to Milosevic. He is told Beara is the person he needs to see. His recollection, then, of meeting this person Beara by name is adequate.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot confirm whether anyone's recollection is adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, the fact pattern. Not -- that's up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm only saying is -- and that refers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor. One minute, please. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to make things clear that my colleague said that the Nikolic team had not contested the fact that Drago Nikolic had done something. The fact that we did not contest the identity of the man to whom he was referred does not mean that we accept in any way or that we recognise in any way who Drago Nikolic might have sent this man if he was seen, if he was seen by Marko Milosevic. So there is no absolutely no acquiescence on our part that Beara was ever there at that moment, and there's no, either, any recognition on our part that Drago Nikolic was ever there. We simply asked the man, was the man that you -- that encounter, that Marko Milosevic spoke about, where did it take place? Nothing else. There's no -- absolutely no acceptance on our part of any of that evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly not put to the witness in cross-examination that Drago Nikolic was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the point I was asking my colleagues about, but we have noted the position of the each parties. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, you have no idea whether Milosevic met Colonel Beara that day?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no opinion on that, and as I was saying, and this reflects -- relates to all witnesses, the only thing I'm saying, that if there is a question about encounters either because it is challenged by one of the parties or even without challenging, if the Court doubts such an encounter, in that case it is -- the table explains in which way certain witnesses could have testified further. That's all. I'm not taking any position on whether encounters took place or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think we're to the last one of the seven who you say could have been tested, and that is PW 104, the last one on your table.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Interviewed on the 7th and 9th of April, 2006. Now, we've discussed wanted posters, media exposure, et cetera. At this point Mr. Beara is in custody here, so without belabouring it that would be a reason not to test this witness who resides in a region and could have been exposed?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. If that was the first time that this witness was found, it was too late to test him further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is another witness where you say that there is all the more reason to test this witness because of the denial of having seen any glasses and that this invokes questions about the accuracy of their observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I suppose just to be safe, can we go into private session for a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he testified in this case of his meeting with Beara and the Zvornik brigade command. At 7941, he said: "I know that I was there as well as the officer who introduced himself as Colonel Beara." That recollection of Beara introducing himself is also in the interview 2466, which I've referenced at page 2. Now, I think I can do this in open session. In 65 ter number 2466 under seal, his 9th of April interview on page 3, he was asked whether Beara wore glasses. His answer was: "I do not remember." He did not deny that Beara wore glasses. He couldn't remember 11 years later. Now, again, why does your report say that he denied that Beara wore glasses when he said he couldn't recall?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's the same question you've asked before, that sentence you've read. He denied remembering glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you've testified and said a couple of times, I think, that you have no way of knowing whether Mr. Beara always wore glasses?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not within my field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, may not be within your field of expertise, but you are also saying that you weren't -- you don't have that information?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is the only pictures that I have seen were pictures where he was wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Until today?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, the witness here, PW 104, he said -- as I've read out said: "He did not look the same as the guy in The Hague. He was bigger, well built." That is 9 April interview, 2466 under seal at page 3. And he described that meeting, as I've said, as one standing up. So how does that affect the memory, Professor, face to face with Mr. Beara in a very disturbing meeting, this colonel standing over him? That can create the appearance of remembering somebody as big if you are face-to-face with him in a standing meeting and they are much larger than you, correct? Would that be one of the significant things you would remember, you talked about, you know, hair and things like that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're asking -- you're referring to a few different problems. One is the impression a person makes at a disturbing meeting, and the other question seems to be whether you would recognise a person after so many years when he changed considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's not it. Let me break it down and make it simpler. Forget the disturbing or the nature of the meeting. You talked yesterday - I think my colleague Mr. Bourgon asked you; I can't remember who - well, if someone was asked to remember you what would they remember, and you described, you know, your hair and somewhat your age, things like that. You're not too big, you're not too small, things like that. If a person is meeting somebody face to face standing up who is bigger than them, would that be one of those characteristics that would likely be recalled?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we must make a breakdown between things you store in memory at the moment and things that will be recalled after a long interval. There's a difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you can explain that.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I try to explain, what is your question about? Is it what will a person store in memory at that moment or what will a person remember of all those memories stored after 12 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean later because he can't remember it later unless you store it in the first place, so what I'm saying is -- I see your point. When you store the memory that this person was a lot bigger than you, and if you did, is that in the category of things that you might recall years later in describing the person?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That depends on the person who is doing the storage. If you are yourself not a very tall person, you will have the experience that many people you meet are taller than you. That's not so special. So a shorter person would store the memory of a person taller than me especially if there is just a very large remarkable difference. A very tall person, if he meets someone who is really much taller than himself, would notice that immediately because that doesn't happen so often. So it depends a lot on who is doing the storing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm talking now the fact that I'm a smaller person with a taller person.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It if the witness is a smaller person, he would not have been so surprised that others are taller than himself, and that might not have been a very special feature that he would remember. If the person he met is much, much longer than others, his smaller posture would not make it difficult for him as for anyone else to notice that he's meeting an especially tall person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And other people have described Mr. Beara as big as part of their descriptions.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, and that's what this witness also says, so there's no discrepancy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And in his testimony, which is at 8014, on cross-examination he was asked to describe the Mr. Beara, the Colonel Beara who introduced himself to him in this meeting, and he said tall, camouflage uniform, well built, grey hair, age around 50, 55. Now, here's another interesting point I want to ask you about. At transcript reference 8015, the witness in this transcript was provided to you, he said that he saw Beara on television at the time of his transfer to The Hague, which is before we interviewed him. So even there with the information provided to you, you could have concluded that it would violate Rule 1 to have conducted a lineup test?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To have conducted a lineup test at that moment, yeah. A lineup test should have been conducted before he saw pictures of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So we can agree that a lineup test should not have been conducted of this witness considering the time he was interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment not, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, I'd like to look at a short video. That's 3660. And this is video of Mr. Beara at some stage. It's a news report of his transfer to The Hague. PW 104 describes seeing television footage of Mr. Beara coming to The Hague. I can't say this is exactly the same, but it's footage of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that the time to the witness that he saw Mr. Beara in July 1995, Beara in his camouflage uniform in this face-to-face meeting did appear to him bigger, well built than the man he saw nine, ten years later coming to The Hague in a suit?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain what you're actually asking. The witness said he looked different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. So --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no way I can contradict that if he says that's what -- that's his feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but my point is, that can be a witness in his testimony being scrupulously honest when he says the 56-year-old man he saw and spoke with in 1995 in the flesh in this meeting did not look the same to him as the approximately 65-year-old man he saw on TV in a suit.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That could be just purely straight, honest testimony: He looked different. It doesn't mean that there's a problem, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear from this testimony what he's actually saying. Is he saying, I see it's the same man but he has changed, which is possible psychologically, that you can recognise someone after 12 years and also see that someone has changed; or is he saying, he looks so different from me, I wouldn't have noticed it's the same person. It's not clear to me exactly what he's saying. I only know what he says, which is he looks different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that he can't say is that man --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can see good reasons why he's saying that because he also looks different to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's show a quick video now, 3638. This is the clip you've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, that's an image from much earlier. They do look different, don't they?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it you are proposing that the person we saw is Mr. Beara because, of course, I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me continue then. Now, I am talking now about glasses. We saw the video clip of Mr. Beara coming to The Hague, and you could see there that at that point when he was in the room walking around, talking to people, hugging people, then climbing the steps to the plane, he wasn't wearing glasses, was he?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you again 3644. All right, now. That's the picture we saw before. Looks like it's from the video of Mr. Beara not wearing glasses. You've testified several times you had no way of knowing whether Beara wore glasses - constantly, at least, constantly - and that you hadn't seen him in pictures without glasses in the family pictures provided by the Defence. So they didn't show you this photo. I'd like to look at 3695, please. We are waiting for that to come up. This is that photo of Mr. Beara without glasses that came up while I was preparing your testimony, Professor. This is a Google screen print. That photo's there on the top right, Mr. Beara without glasses. It's also on the second row. That's actually there three times. So you can see this was searched on Google images under the phrase "Ljubisa Beara." It took .02 seconds to come up. That's the time. So --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when was this consulted, this Google? You always need dates when you get things from the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have the date on it, but this was last week.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is essential. There's no way to know what was available on Google, say, the month before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's true, but the news story that is coming up is a 2004 story, so if it wasn't available it was taken off and then somehow put back up. But my point is, did anybody from the Defence or you take that less than a second to check for other images to see whether Beara might -- there might be photos of him not wearing glasses?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why I asked for the date is that, in fact, I did. Although it's not part of my report, I did, and I do not not remember, but I can only draw from my memory what I saw because I did not make a print because if I had made a print I would have supplied it to you as part of my notes. But I did do that, and I do not remember it, so -- but my memory can be wrong, so that's why I was interested in the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, actually, this one, for the record, Ms. Stewart has helpfully checked the myth when this was printed. It was put in our records. It was 4th September. Very quickly, let's go back --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I started to work on this report in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's got to 3 --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would be very pleased if you could improve my memory by showing the thing I've seen in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 3644, please, back there again for one minute. I'll see if I can help. Okay. This is from the internet. I don't know exactly when we found it, but it's from a news site. It comes up if you search "Ljubisa Beara." Can we go up to the top. This is an archive from Vreme, I probably pronounced that wrong, Vreme, 14 October 2004. So I can't prove it, but my guess is this didn't disappear for just that minute of time -- that portion of time and come back up, so that would have been available to you and to the Defence, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no way of checking whether this was available on Google or not. The only thing I can affirm is that, indeed, I looked at Google, and I don't remember seeing pictures of Mr. Beara without glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me now move to the -- continuing on the glasses, I want to show you the interview of witness Celanovic. This was in your binder of material. It was made available to you. You discussed Celanovic's meeting with Beara in Bratunac, and you say he should not be tested because he was familiar with Mr. Beara. In fact, he was very familiar. Can we have 65 ter 3694 up, please, at page 15. It talks a bit about his familiarity there, and actually, this is from your binders. I don't need to put it on ELMO. I don't think -- this section is actually highlighted in the materials you have. And on page 15, Mr. Celanovic says, speaking of Beara: "I knew him from before because he visited the brigade several times, so he came -- he mainly came for Major Nikolic, because he was a security body higher than him, and he would come -- he came to me, to my office, and he came -- both of them came several times being interested in how many criminal reports there are, how many cases have been solved or processed by the Bijeljina corps, and that was the reason they would come to me." That's probably why he found him familiar and, therefore, should not be tested with a photo lineup. Let's go to page 25, please. And if you want to look, Professor, in your binders or take my word for it, if you prefer, this section is highlighted.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And here the investigator, Allistair Graham has some more questions ten pages later about Mr. Beara. Mr. Graham says: "Okay. Just getting back to Beara. To make sure we're talking about the same person, can you just describe him to me?" No leading questions there. "Answer: Ljubisa Beara, lieutenant-colonel, I have the information he was in the Main Staff, the main officer for security. "Can you describe him for me? "Answer: A strong built, tall man. He was -- had a receding hair, or had receding hair, greyish or grey hair. Sometimes he had glasses, sometimes not." You had available to you clear, unambiguous information from a recognition witness that Colonel Beara sometimes wore glasses and sometimes he didn't. Let me look at your 65 ter summary 3696 at page 8. Please don't broadcast the first page. Let's wait for that to come up. Bottom section, "glasses": "Says Beara only wore glasses sometimes, and sometimes he did not." Can I have 3704 up, please. Those are your handwritten notes that you've been reading from in your testimony. This should not be broadcast. Should not be broadcast. Number 5, "Celanovic. Familiar, receding greyish hair, sometimes glasses." You have had that information in front of you while you're testifying here. You've had it in your summaries. You've had this statement. You said you have no way of knowing whether he wore glasses or not. That wasn't quite correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see why you're saying that. Are you saying that I should accept as an authority a witness who makes a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying Professor, is --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know whom to believe. If I should make an assertion, accept as a scientific fact at the basis of my analyses that he always wore glasses or never or sometimes, I need independent information, not from 1 out of 12 witnesses who says something. That is not a fact. When a witness says something, the scientific fact is that the witness says something, but through that I cannot establish scientifically that he wore glasses or not, and I don't think I've misled anyone about that. It's in my notes. I -- nowhere have I said in my report that Mr. Beara was always wearing glasses. I said I have no scientific basis to assume what the actual condition is. And if this is a point that is in doubt, if it is challenged by one party or another, then there are means to resolve that question. Maybe identification methods could be helpful there, although I'm not absolutely sure that it would be helpful. I only can say if that is in doubt, and there's some reason for doubt because not all witnesses say sometimes he wore glasses, sometimes he didn't -- not, witnesses say all sorts of things about glasses. I can only present to the Court that there is a point to be resolved but not through my science and definitely not by just encouraging the Court to accept one testimony instead of the others. I can only note what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, here's the problem, Professor, as I see it. You and the Defence have made sort of a big deal about glasses in this, in your report, and in your testimony. You've talked about, and you did this the other day, that it can be a problem if some witnesses see the individual wearing glasses and some don't, and in all those cases you're talking about what you've read in the materials that were provided to you. And the one piece of information that you didn't provide to the Court that was material provided to you that you read was that, well, one recognition witness who was very familiar says that sometimes he did wear glasses and sometimes he didn't, and he provided that answer in a completely non-leading way when asked to describe. So my question is, you've read all these witness statements; you have this in front of you; the Court doesn't have that witness statement. I don't know if you know that. That hadn't been put into evidence. Wouldn't it be helpful to the Court when you're discussing what all the witnesses say about glasses to also mention that one witness says, sometimes he wore them, sometimes he didn't? Wouldn't that when you're talking about glasses add that one piece of info?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that piece of information is in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last paragraph of the last page says, in a summary statement, Witnesses number 135, 113 - that's Celanovic - 21, and 157 say that the person they saw did not or not continually wear glasses. I'm not implying here that all witnesses say exactly the same. I say this is the sort of variety that was of statements about glasses that was proposed by these witnesses. I'm not a Defence attorney, and I'm definitely not the Court. I think this is a sufficient indication for the Court to look exactly at the statements these witnesses made. 113 is in this list. If you're telling me the Court has no access to the statements made by the witness Celanovic, then I would be surprised. I had access to it, and I can't see why the Court would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say there in the sentence you've read out, the next sentence says: "Especially the testimony of witnesses including 113 invoke questions about the accuracy of their observations." Now, what is it about Mr. Celanovic saying sometimes he wore glasses, sometimes he didn't that raises questions about the accuracy of his observations because this is couched as that it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're -- there's a bit of confusion. You tell me that I must accept as a fact that Witness 113 is very familiar with Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've classified him as familiar.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said I must classify him as familiar because that's what he claims. I also said in my report quite clear that the question of familiarity must be investigated carefully because there can be good reasons for witnesses who are familiar to deny familiarity and witnesses who are unfamiliar to claim familiarity. I stress especially the point that that is a point to be investigated by the Court, and there's no way for me to give answers to that question or to confirm on the basis of my science that, indeed, this witness was familiar. I can only say how he must be classified according to his statements. But if my table, the column with unknown/familiar, would be interpreted by you as the outcome of a scientific study that tells the Court the truth about familiarity, I must say you are utterly mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm getting towards the end. I'm moving on now. We've gone through these seven ones who you initially said should have been tested, and you've agreed with me that some of them perhaps should not. I'm going to look now at known recognitions. These are Milorad Bircakovic, Celanovic who we've just discussed, and (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take care of it. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They cannot be tested because of their familiarity. Now, for Celanovic and PW 161, and this was a statement highlighted by my friend Mr. Ostojic, he said there seems to be little -- no, actually, this is the one he missed. He went to the next sentence. This is the sentence I want to highlight: "There seems to be little doubt that conditions for an accurate observation were present." He didn't read that sentence. He read the next sentence. "However, it should be realized that without such a sensitive test as a proper lineup, it cannot really be decided whether their claimed recognition really took place..." which is what you've just said. "They might be mistaken and they might lie about it." Do you really think the judges, professional judges of this Court, need an expert to tell them that a witness can make a mistake or might tell a lie?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a difficult question. What I think the Court needs to be informed about and whatnot -- in fact, a major part of my report I think the Court doesn't need to be informed about because I hope it is within the realm of professional knowledge of a Court. And if I would have followed that judgement, there would be hardly any report. This argument is even stronger if it's realized that I report about similar matters a number of times before. So I have already accepted that in these reports, 80 percent of what I say is stating the obvious, anyway. This is even more true for the Prosecution because there's only one office of the Prosecutor, and you cite and have cited a number of times from my previous reports, which the Court will probably find more difficult to do because they have not attended these other trials, but you did. So for the same reason you could have asked me, why did I describe the rules for the first time, and indeed, it is my feeling that for this Tribunal I am more or less repeating myself a number of times and really do not have a new message. So having come to the point that I describe exactly the same rules again for this Tribunal, I have long overcome the hesitation of stating something that, of course, is obvious to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, I just want to talk to you a little bit about Mr. Bircakovic, who is Witness number 142, the third one down on your table. Only a few questions, and I'm -- you may be able to help me here because I was puzzled. You'll -- and he's a familiar witness, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says he was familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He says he was familiar. Your report states: "For the three witnesses who were already familiar" -- and this is on page 10 under Section 4. "For the three witnesses who are already familiar with Beara, no formal identity test can be held. The only thing that can be judged is whether the conditions described by them would allow a reliable recognition. For Witness 142, this seems not to be the case, as he was not even certain that he met Mr. Beara." And you said yesterday at 25339, I quote your answer: "Well, Mr. Bircakovic did not positively say he saw Mr. Beara at a certain place, a person well known to him. He said he may have seen him but that's not -- but he's not certain who he saw." And I'm going to try to unpack this a little bit and see where you get this from. In your summaries, which we don't need to bring up, 65 ter 3696 - we don't need to bring it up unless you want to - it also says for Bircakovic, not even certain that he met with Mr. Beara. And your table in your report at page 9 says may have seen him. Now, in your summaries you cite to transcript reference 11097 at line 12. And this is the section -- sorry, let me change that. I'm sorry. I made a mistake. That's not what you cite in your summaries. Let me read to you from transcript 11097. "Question: Now, in the years that you were a driver for superior officers, would you agree with me, sir, as a common soldier and driver that it is not common that a person in your position as such a driver and a common soldier would be told the reason that you were going to fetch somebody or pick somebody up or bring another superior officer somewhere, what the purpose of what they were going to do would be? "Answer: Well, it was not an order back then. When Popovic and Beara arrived at the barracks, everybody saw it. It wasn't concealed. It wasn't being hidden. I was told. Of course, when there were meetings held then there was no such talk." So the question there was about whether he was told the reason he was going to go and pick up someone, Drago Nikolic, and he says in his answer everybody saw when they arrived, and he is referring to being told about the meeting. Where is he saying he's not certain in that answer that he saw Beara?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is going too fast. I don't get the text on my video, which makes it very difficult because this is about precise interpretation of words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I see what we have up here?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Now I can read it. If you just allow me a second, I will read that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So what I read is: "When Popovic and Beara arrived at the barracks, everybody saw it. It wasn't concealed. It wasn't being hidden. I was told."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told what? That this was Mr. Beara, or did he recognise Mr. Beara then because he was a well known figure or because he knew Mr. Beara personally? What exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is interpreted, I was told that that was Mr. Beara or I was told Mr. Beara would come and I saw someone, that's not logically conclusive. Then we are still not certain whom he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If you -- do you think --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if a number of persons arrive and I'm told Mr. Beara is one of them, it's still not certain that I picked out the right one and now know what Mr. Beara looks like. So this is not a logically conclusive statement, and that's why I said it's possible that in fact he was told it was Beara but it wasn't, or it was told it was Beara or he looked at the wrong person. It cannot be, and that's why I say familiarity needs to be investigated very carefully because some people claim to have seen someone before, whereas in fact the person they saw was someone else and they're wrong about familiarity. Easy familiarity is like in the case of Tadic where people say we lived with him in the same village for 25 years, I was training in his sports school. But this type of encounter where people are told things is less certain; and therefore, you need to investigate familiarity in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So -- last question before the break, I think. So you are not taking into account the question where he's asked whether he would be told about the reason to pick somebody up? That's the question about being told, and he says I was told.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that Mr. Beara would come. But that doesn't make sure for me that the person who arrived was in fact Mr. Beara or when more than one person arrived that he knew which one of those people would be Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look at some more of this testimony after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It won't be very much longer, Your Honours. This is the last chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Maybe 15 minutes. 10, 15 minutes. Depends on the answers a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long, Mr. Ostojic, do you plan to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would hope to conclude today, but I would need about a half hour, and I would also ask the Court if the times are accurate if we should release the witness that's been waiting since 11, I think, or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do that. Thank you, we'll be adjourned for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we have 3696 up, please. Those are the summaries at page 6. Thanks. Now, just so we can see that, Professor, that's your summary where you cite through your -- the portions you used for the Bircakovic analysis, and we just went through the first one, transcript reference 11097, the one we were discussing as one of your cites. Let's go now, quickly, to 1107, line 5. That's the next cite in the transcript, and that portion goes as follows. That line's -- there the question goes -- 1107, line 5. The question is about seeing Mr. Beara at the standard building early in the morning on the 14th, and the answer is -- the question was whether he was seen by the school. "I said no. He did not ask me anything else." Now, there the witness Bircakovic says that he was asked about the school, and said he didn't see Mr. Beara at the school, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That doesn't -- I'll just continue. You also cite to Mr. Bircakovic's OTP interview at page 38, lines 15 to 17. That's 65 ter 4D00105, and we can bring that up if we need to. And the lines aren't actually on this page in the materials you were given, but if you read this, Professor, the interviewer, Mr. Manning, asked Bircakovic: "Were you present during the meeting? "No. "Who was president [sic]? "There was Popovic and there was Beara present at the meeting. "Was Trbic also present?" "I do not know." There, Professor, the only thing we see is Bircakovic says that he was not in the meeting between Drago Nikolic, Beara, and Popovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were given a supplemental information sheet, that's 65 ter 3705. If we could bring that up on page 2. This is from the 6th of May, 2007. It's not on your screen yet. That may be difficult for you to read. I'm interested in the fourth paragraph. I'll read it out: "The witness was asked if he recalled what type of uniforms Beara and Popovic were wearing at the Zvornik brigade headquarters on the morning of 14 July. He stated that he thought that Beara and Popovic were wearing camouflage uniforms during their 14 July, 9 or 10 a.m. meeting with Nikolic at the Zvornik brigade headquarters. The witness knew Popovic from trips to the Drina corps, and he also knew Beara from earlier." Now, there does the witness sound that he is uncertain of whether he saw Beara?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me point you to a couple of sections of the cross-examination by Bircakovic by counsel for Mr. Beara. These are not referenced in your report. This is at transcript page 1102 of our trial. Question by Christopher Meeks: "You also stated after that when again talking about whether Trbic was in the meeting, you said you didn't know who was in that room because you weren't there. Isn't that correct?" "Answer: I didn't go in, but in the morning when I arrived, Popovic and Beara arrived, as well, so they went into the barracks and I saw them go in." Now, how does that "I saw them go in" get translated into your testimony and your report that he was not certain?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my report, of course, in a very summarily way reflects various statements made by this witness, and you correctly cited that on the 14th of -- that in the supplemental information sheet he had said he was sure that he did not observe Beara at the Orahovac school on the 14th of July. So there is a question to be resolved, which of those statements actually reflects the true condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not to decide which of all that are true. I can only say if there is a question - and there seems to be a question because he doesn't seem to be completely consistent - if there is a question, one way to resolve that is through identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, except that he's familiar. But let me -- I think I can help you. There are three issues at play here. One, there's a question of whether the witness Bircakovic saw Beara arriving at the Zvornik brigade headquarters, that's an army headquarters in the morning. He says, yes, I saw them go in. Two is whether Mr. Bircakovic saw Beara in the meeting, in a meeting after he arrived with Drago Nikolic and Popovic. He there says, no, I wasn't in that meeting. The third issue is later in that same day at a different place, an execution site there was a question of whether -- not a execution site, sorry, a detention site whether Mr. Bircakovic saw Mr. Beara at the school, and he says, no, he wasn't at the school. So that may have confused it somewhat. I'm not sure if it was clear from the transcript there are three separate places we're talking about. But the point I was drawing your attention to is that when the witness says regarding arriving at the brigade headquarters, I saw them go in, that doesn't raise a question about his certainty of whether he saw them, which is what you said yesterday in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I can see where there could be a confusion there. The problem is, though, that this witness claims that he knew Mr. Beara from before. I'm not certain to which prior encounter that is referring because there's no clear statement about I knew him very well because I've met him there and there. The only logical conclusion that I can make is that this prior encounter, that that's the first event he mentioned. And then the second encounter --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I stop you for one moment because this may help. We've gone through your binders. For some reason you were not given Mr. Bircakovic's direct testimony, okay? This is page 11012. And in there at the beginning of his testimony on direct, he is asked: "And finally, Ljubisa Beara, did you know him in July 1995?" And he says: "Yes, I did see him around." What was his position? He was chief of security testify Main Staff. So he had -- that wasn't available to you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but that also does not resolve my question. It simply says, I know him, he was around. But that doesn't explain how he know him and how he know that the person around was Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I can't know whether -- what he is referring to because in July 1995 as you've described, there might have been three meetings. The first meeting of those might be the meeting in which he got to know him, so that later on in other meetings he was familiar but not in the first one. That has to be investigated how exactly it went, and a general statement about I met him in July, I knew him, he was around, doesn't explain how he became familiar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I'm talking to you about the certainty issue. The witness has testified that he was familiar with Beara, which is why he could not be tested. Transcript reference 11113, it's another part of the transcript. You did have this. It's cross-examination. You didn't cite. The final question by Chris Meeks: "Well, sir, I'm going to suggest to you that you never saw Ljubisa Beara on the 14th in the morning at the standard building as you first testified about today because he was not there. He was at black river on the 13th and 14th, and I put it to you, sir, that you are not speaking the truth here, just like you didn't speak the truth on these exhibits, on the logbooks because it means nothing to you to tell the truth or to tell a lie. Isn't that correct, sir?" It's been suggested to him that he couldn't have seen Mr. Beara because Mr. Beara was at Main Staff headquarters on the 13th and 14th. And he says: "No." He flat-out denies the charge that he didn't see Beara on the 14th in the morning at standard barracks. There's nowhere -- there's no uncertainty in that answer, is there?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no uncertainty about what he intends to say. The uncertainty relates to whether that's a true statement or not, and that's what the Court needs to investigate. I don't think there is a dispute about what the witness said. The dispute is about whether that's the truth or not, and I'm trying to help the Court find methods to test what witnesses are saying. So I can only say that he affirms that he was there. But that doesn't mean that in my work I should use that as a starting point and accept that he was there and saw Mr. Beara because that's accepting the thing that exactly needs to be proven in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But let me go back to page 10 of your report, Section 4, for what you wrote, what you told the Court about this witness.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 10, bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "The only thing that can be judged is whether the conditions described by them would allow a reliable recognition. For Witness 142, this seems not to be the case as he was not even certain that he met with Mr. Beara." That line that Bircakovic, that he was not certain is not supported, is it, by what we've gone through?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Then you misread what I'm saying. What I'm trying to explain here is that witnesses can be accepted as being familiar with Beara if it is established that there was at least one encounter, hopefully more, in which they got to know Mr. Beara. What I'm saying for a number 142, that is not sure because that first encounter in which supposedly he became familiar with Mr. Beara, you can't actually be sure whether Mr. Beara was the person he met. I'm not talking about a later encounters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, no, but --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first encounter, which is not at the standard building or the school. I talk about the first encounter in which -- which logically should have been the encounter in which he became familiar with Mr. Beara unless there were also other encounters even before that in which the familiarity was established, but then he doesn't tell us. So there is a question there. It's not certain to me that on the morning of the 14th of July he was already familiar with Mr. Beara so that when he saw him he could at that point recognise him instead of just perceive a person who he later could identify. That's the logical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we're supposed to get that from "he was not even certain that he met Mr. Beara"?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is, in his description, from his description you cannot infer that there is no doubt about who he describes and who he met. He talks about -- let me see. That was on the day he picked up Nikolic and then he saw certain persons, but from his story, it cannot be inferred by me as an absolute fact that from there on that he really met Mr. Beara and from there on he could always recognise him because he now was familiar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but there's nothing --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the type of familiarity we discussed before of, like in the Tadic case, living 25 years in the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if it is a single encounter and it's not quite established what the exact condition of this encounter are, then I think the Court needs to be informed as I did that this whole aspect of familiarity needs to be further investigated. That's the only intention of this sentence. I do not say he's familiar. I do not say he's unfamiliar because that's not my position. I say for number 142, this seems not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you are referring to here is that the conditions for familiarity are not met here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not so certain -- certainly establish that I could use that as a starting point for my further analysis like I did in the Tadic case when a large number of witnesses declared they came from the same village and that was not denied. It's a different situation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you think you can conclude very soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just this, Witness -- Mr. Professor, the first sentence of that question titled "The Three Recognitions" is for the three witnesses who were already familiar with Beara, no formal identification test can be held. So you did categorise him as familiar, and the part of the transcript not given to you by the Defence said that he did know him in July 1995, and I don't think you found anywhere in any of those transcripts or statements anything to suggest that the 14 July 1995 was a first encounter, have you?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I also didn't think I said that, but what I say is that the reason of his familiarity is not clear to me. He only refers to this event where he had to -- he picked up Nikolic. That's what he mentioned as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last question, if I may. Can we have the proofing note up again, 3705. Last question. Paragraph 4 again, talking about the 14 July encounter, last sentence at paragraph 4: "The witness knew Popovic from trips to the Drina Corps, and he also knew Beara from earlier." Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Where are we on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Fourth paragraph down. I can give you a hard copy if nobody minds.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the same. If you're going to -- "type of uniforms."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the paragraph. Last line.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It says, the witness knew Popovic from trips to Drina Corps, but my testimony is not about Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, keep reading.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he also knew Beara from earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As in earlier than 14 July?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But there's no statement about when that was. There are no question about, say, what were the earlier events, what were the conditions which you see him, how did you know then it was Beara, because there's always a first time when you have to learn who someone is. So this really doesn't help me whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I give these back to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just can't promise the Court I'll conclude today, but we'll see how it goes. I'll make every effort to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the Court's aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's take, first, a look at this Google search, 3344, if we may. While that's coming up -- that's the Google search that the Prosecution did, I think he said the 4th of September that seems to depict Mr. Beara in various instances without his glasses, but my question when we get it up is whether or not that's the same picture, just whether it's zoomed in or zoomed out. So in fact I'm suggesting to you, sir, that if we look at that picture -- and that's not it right here, but I will try to get the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll stipulate it's the same picture if that helps him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looked to me it's the same picture. That's what Google does all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's a couple of other pictures of Mr. Beara there as well. Now, if we can go to the video of 3600 and play that. Just -- and I'll ask him when I think you should stop. I don't know if you noticed a couple of things, but as it's coming up I want to ask you this. Although the Prosecution shared with you some of the circumstances upon which that video was taken, but I want you to play close attention to both the bridge of Mr. Beara's nose, and I want you to also pay close attention to his breast pocket. I don't think it's funny, but our position was, Professor, and still is that in July of 1995 for a period ten years prior, Mr. Beara always wore glasses. That's been our position throughout, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object -- I object to that, testifying by counsel. He's never called a witness to say that. He hasn't put it in, and he began his direct by saying, did I ever tell you, Witness, about whether Mr. Beara constantly wore glasses, the witness said, no. He can call a witness. He can't testify about that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we have brought witnesses, but I dare remind my colleague that he has the burden of proof on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But let me go through this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness said that it was not for the witness to testify to that. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And sir, if we -- can we look at that video now, 3660, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Stop it right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see anything in that left breast pocket that you can make out possibly?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, one second before there, you saw a flash suggesting that that might be glasses or at least something that's highly reflecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm sure you're familiar since you wear glasses, there are circumstances someone who always wear glasses may remove them, and not to be facetious, but for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we said that it is not for the witness. We can see the picture. You can make a submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me with this, Professor. Would you agree with me that there are circumstances other than getting a photograph to determine if Mr. Beara actually wore glasses in 1995, and I know you don't -- you may not be familiar with the names of these witness that the Prosecution called, but let's just say if the Prosecution called colleagues of Mr. Beara, people who sat with him during that time on the Main Staff such as Peter Skrbic, Manojlo Milovanovic or even Milomir Savcic, do you think that perhaps those people would know definitively whether or not Mr. Beara wore glasses in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without having to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Without having to hear from Mr. Nicholls, the same applies. Move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look, if you will, Professor, the familiar person that the Prosecution shared with you, and that was Mr. Celanovic, and now he claims -- I think that's the gentleman who says he sometimes wore glasses, sometimes he didn't. But Mr. Celanovic, if we look at that specific page that they had up -- let me just find it so I can share it with you. I think it was Exhibit 3694 if I'm not mistaken. And when we are talking about familiarity with a witness, that witness - I'm just trying to find my notes here, but I think it won't draw an objection - actually identifies Mr. Beara as being of what rank. I think it's two lines, actually, before my learned friend was directing your attention to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my notes, he doesn't remember he was a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, he says plainly there, doesn't he, that he's a lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I should consult -- and you can read as well what -- as I can what he says. In my notes, it said he doesn't remember whether he was a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel, so there was some doubt about the rank at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he says that he has information that he's on the Main Staff, so let's assume for the second that Mr. Celanovic is being truthful and he remembers him as being a lieutenant-colonel, although I think it's pretty well stipulated that Mr. Beara was a colonel since 1985 according to at least the evidence they brought forth. So ten years later, this person claims to have a familiarity with Mr. Beara, this individual Celanovic. He has his rank wrong, and he just has information that he may be on the Main Staff. How well do you think he knows him?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a difficult question, and I don't want to prolong this procedure, but I think that the question needs to be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For military people, ranks are extremely important. You would always know the rank of -- I've been a military person myself. You would always know the exact rank of people, and it would be highly surprising if you made a mistake. But the question is what exactly is Mr. Celanovic? Has he spent a life in military, or is he one of those person who joins some army group lately and is not very familiar with ranks? If you want to know what it means, if he confuses lieutenant-colonel and a colonel, which have same word in it, then you must know how experienced a military person Mr. Celanovic is. So I can't make --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please switch off his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I cannot interpret, and I think also the Court cannot interpret that confusion without knowing exactly what Mr. Celanovic experienced as a military is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well -- and not to belabour the point, but just so I have it. I want to look at page 25 of Exhibit 3694, which is this interview with him, and specifically I'm going to draw your attention to the two lines prior to what my colleague asked you about, and it talks about how fair the question was, just describe him and how it wasn't a leading question, and then he goes on on line 8, the answer by Mr. Celanovic: "Ljubisa Beara, lieutenant-colonel, I have the information that he was in the Main Staff, the main officer for security." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I just wanted to direct your attention to. Now, let's go and continue on this line that the Prosecutor had as to how fair their questions may have been to witnesses. Now, in circumstances such as Mr. Egbers, he claims that he met a person that we've come here to call, Major Zoran or Zoran Malinic, okay? Do you think that his interview, since Captain Egbers said that he was present with Major Zoran, might be relevant to whether or not Captain Zoran Malinic can confirm whether Beara was there or not at Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it for the witness to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would beg to differ. I don't think that has a whole lot to do with memory and perception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it is not for the witness to answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to stick with Mr. Egbers if we can, Professor. I'm suggesting to you that the Prosecution, when they had his interviews, at some point he claims that he was introduced to Mr. Beara; at other points in his statement, he claims that he was introduced or just -- an interpreter pointed him out as he was coming out of the car. At other points, he states that Mr. Beara introduced himself to him, and let me go through with you if I may. Can we have 2D19, please, which is the October 24, 1995, interview. I just want to see how the progress of these investigations occur, and we'll take this one, which is the 24th of October, 1995. Page 7, please. It's actually the first full paragraph which starts on Friday, and it goes actually five lines down, which is the last sentence in that. It says: "The interpreter told me his name." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we turn to Exhibit 2D20, and I apologise if we're going a little too fast. And for 2D20, we would like to highlight page 3. I believe it should be the third full paragraph, and it's that third paragraph -- full paragraph, I should say, that starts: "Next morning..." It's actually the third line, which states: "The interpreter told me that he was Colonel Beara." Okay? So this is a 1999 interview. We saw the 1995 interview. Now, let's see what he says on the 30th of April, 2000, which is 2D21. Approximately five years after his first interview, here's what Mr. Egbers says about whether the interpreter told him his name as he said on the 24th of October, 1995, as well as on July 1999. On the 30th of April, 2002, again with the OTP, he states -- I'm just trying to find it. It's in the second paragraph, the last line, actually. There's only one -- I think it's page 2. I'm sorry. That second paragraph, the last line, it says: "He introduced himself as Colonel Beara." And then it goes on, and then he says that his impression was -- and we won't talk about that, and we'll address that with the Court later. But five years after the events, now he's saying that Mr. Beara introduced himself, although he gave at least two, but we'll go over it, and I'm not asking -- how good is his recollection, and let's talk about memory, based on this alone?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I think the question needs to be answered, but maybe it's not a short answer. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do as far as you can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to interpret what's going on in the head of the witness Egbers and how he uses his memory, we need to know more about Mr. Egbers. One crucial question is, does he speak Serb-Croatian or not? The mention of an interpreter suggests that he might not, which means that if he didn't, he would never speak directly to Mr. Beara. He could only speak through the interpreter. In that case, the situation could easily have been Mr. Beara introduces himself, the interpreter translates it, so that both statements are true. Mr. Beara introduces himself, and the interpreter tells Mr. Egbers, this is Mr. Beara. The interpreter should not do that. A good interpreter should say, I am Mr. Beara, but that leads to confusions because the interpreter is not Mr. Beara. So -- and it's also possible as you seem to suggest that, first, Egbers remembers that Beara -- that interpreter says, this is Mr. Beara, please speak to him, and that Mr. Beara then doesn't introduce himself anymore, and that Egbers lately incorrectly remembers that Beara introduced himself. That's also possible. The uncertainty about this situation is due to the fact that it was never asked to Mr. Egbers, could you speak directly to him, what do you mean when he said he introduced himself, do you speak Serbo-Croatian, or do you mean, he did that, and then the interpreter translated for you? It's a very unclear situation, and I can only come to the conclusion as a scientist, for me that's not sufficient information to interpret what has happened in his memory or how he's used the memory. If it is sufficient for the finder of fact, I have no comment on that. It's not for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, Professor, thank you, and I think I understand what you mean when you say uncertainty and unclear, and I believe all of us do. But let me show you one other exhibit, 2D22, if I may. And this is another -- it's an interview from the ICTY conducted by the investigators and whatnot, and it's of a UN peacekeeping interview questionnaire is the caption. And if we can just speed along and go to page 3 of that.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're still talking about Mr. Egbers, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Now, let's look at page 3. If we could just scroll down, although Mr. Beara's name is mentioned on top, and we could discuss with you whether Mr. Egbers in some of his statements says he personally contacted Beara, although here he says that Major Zoran was contacting him, couldn't get a hold of him, but that's not really what my question is. It's really below there, a pretty straightforward question to Mr. Egbers: "Did you at any stage see General Mladic or any of his corps commanders?" And then there's some explanation by the questionnaire apparently. The answer is: "No", and then there's some space, and he writes: "Perhaps Colonel Beara." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that go to what you just said, that uncertainty and unclarity?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's suggested at the time he answered this question that he wasn't quite sure -- well, that -- even the answer is unclear because it isn't -- from the answer it does not appear what the source of his uncertainty is. Is he certain he met a person but he doesn't know for sure that was Colonel Beara, or is he not even certain he met any high-ranked officer at all? It's very short and, of course, he should have asked, why do you say "perhaps"? What is exactly the source of your uncertainty? What are you uncertain about? So that leaves open all sorts of possibilities, also the possibility that he met with a high-ranked officer, he knows that for certain, but he doesn't -- he's not completely certain who that person was. That's one of the possible interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they're reasonable possibilities or reasonable interpretations, are they not, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no opinion about what is reasonable or not. It's a possibility, and I've no way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- preferring one over the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have just a few other areas to cover with you, so I don't mean to interrupt you, Professor, because -- and you've been very patient with us, and thank you for that. Let's talk about what my learned friend said with respect to Mr. Babic today. It's one of the witnesses, and if we could just look at -- I don't know if you can, but page 21, line 16. He starts by saying: "Witness gives a description..." and then this is what my learned friend said about testimony that I want to elicit from you. He says: "I won't bother reading it." Relating to Babic. I'm going to let you catch up. But you can look at your summary sheet that you have on Babic, and you let me know when you've caught up with me.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my summary sheet here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we are going to get to it in the transcript. Now, I'm not going to ask you why he didn't want to read that description that Mr. Babic gives of this purported sighting or visit with Mr. Beara, but why don't you tell us because it does bother me that this -- because I think descriptions are important. Tell us what -- in the evidence you reviewed, what is the description that Mr. Babic gives of purportedly seeing Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my notes, it said, witness described Beara was blond with fair hair, hair was not thick, was very short in the back -- the hair, he meant, I think. He had a receding hairline, combed over, very neatly shaved, no mustache, no glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have a page citation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you have a page citation for that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the transcript page 10240/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To help my friend, it's page 5, paragraph 8 of the statement, which is what I cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that description -- is that a fair and accurate description if we wanted to attest or assert whether someone looks like that? He -- strike that. I apologise. It's getting late. Is that a description that we can utilize to determine whether or not the person Mr. Babic was with was actually Mr. Beara if we have his characteristics or descriptions?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in the business of matching descriptions with actual people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I finish my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best way -- the best way to use this description, I said, we can use that as a starting point for constructing a lineup, and then if the witness identifies someone from a lineup of people all fitting the description, then in my science you may conclude that it's a fair description of Mr. Beara whom he singled out. That's how we do it, and we don't do it -- we make the -- do not make the direct jump. If you would make the direct jump from a description to asserting this must have been Mr. Beara, you would never need lineups in the first place. So that's not how we do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the way you're suggesting is the proper way to do it, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my science, we call that the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask one other quick question if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness are kindly asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just put one more question, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have more?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, actually. And I'm sorry, and I just want -- also, if we could ask the witness if he is even available tomorrow, and I just don't know that because I haven't spoken to him in close to a week other than here in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, would you be available tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fortunately, you do not ask me whether I would be delighted, but the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without delight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll try to make it delightful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But if I could ask this question: My learned friend of the Prosecution showed us some wanted posters, and we're all familiar with that from time to time, but is -- am I correct that the threshold question if there are wanted posers of every witness is to determine whether or not they actually viewed a photograph or a wanted poster which may bear a photograph of a person they claim to have either recognised or identified? Is that a threshold question?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by a threshold question. The situation is that if posters are placed in such a way that witnesses have possibly seen them, then asking the witnesses did you see them does not really resolve the question whether they saw them. It only resolves the question whether they remembered seeing them. But even if they did not remember seeing them, they might still have seen them, and unconsciously the information that they gained, essentially, could unconsciously be used in a lineup. So establishing the logical possibility that they might have seen photographs, that's the threshold question. And what they remember about seeing relates to the same frailty of memory as other statements of a witness. And my position is that if witness makes statements about things they seem to remember, you might do well by testing, finding accurate test for some of the things they claim; and therefore, it should not be accepted as a fact when witnesses say, I never saw those posters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, and again, for agreeing to come back tomorrow. I'm sorry, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be it for today, and my apology to Professor for not being able to keep our Presiding Judge's promise this morning. We'll meet again tomorrow morning. Our thanks go to the Prlic Trial Chamber for kindly changing the courtroom time again. 9 o'clock tomorrow morning.
